question: Where is the majority of the fluid in your body actually stored?
explanation: Great job! Most of our body water is kept safely tucked away right inside our cells (intracellular fluid). Think of it as the main water reservoir of the body!

question: Roughly what fraction of your total body water lives outside the cells (extracellular fluid)?
explanation: Spot on! About one-third of our body fluid flows outside the cells, while the other two-thirds stays safely inside. You've got this!

question: Which electrolyte is the main boss outside the body cells, keeping fluid volumes in check?
explanation: You got it! Sodium is the primary ion outside our cells. It loves water and plays a huge role in keeping our fluid levels balanced.

question: Why is keeping enough potassium inside the cells so crucial for your patients?

options.A: It directly controls blood pressure in the arteries
options.B: It prevents the kidneys from producing too much urine
options.C: It regulates red blood cell production in bone marrow
options.D: It maintains stable heart rhythm and muscle action

explanation: Exactly! Potassium is a heart-loving electrolyte. When potassium levels go out of whack, the heart and muscles can struggle to beat properly.

question: In simple terms, what is osmosis?

options.A: The active pumping of mineral particles out of a cell using energy
options.B: The settling of heavy mineral solutes at the bottom of a container
options.C: The movement of blood cells through tiny capillary walls
options.D: The movement of water across a membrane toward higher solute concentration

explanation: Spot on! Water naturally moves toward areas with more solutes (like salt or sugar) to try and balance things out. Water always follows where the crowd is thickest!

question: What physical pushing force drives fluid and tiny particles out of blood capillaries and into tissues?
explanation: You nailed it! Hydrostatic pressure is simply the physical pushing pressure of blood flowing through your vessels, forcing fluid out into the tissues.

question: What is the main job of Antidiuretic Hormone (ADH) when your body needs to hold onto water?

options.A: It blocks the sensation of thirst in the brain
options.B: It increases the excretion of sodium in the urine
options.C: It promotes water reabsorption back into the blood
options.D: It stimulates the adrenal glands to release aldosterone

explanation: Great work! ADH acts like a conservation officer in your kidneys, telling them to save water and make your urine concentrated so you don't dry out.

question: If a patient has too much fluid and their heart chambers are stretched, which hormone does the heart release to get rid of the extra water?
explanation: You got it! When the heart feels stretched out from too much fluid, it releases ANP to tell the kidneys, 'Time to flush out extra salt and water!'

question: Which organ does the heavy lifting when it comes to adjusting and managing your daily fluid loss?
explanation: Spot on! The kidneys are the ultimate fluid supervisors, tweaking how much water leaves your body every single day through urine.

question: A patient with a fever is breathing fast and sweating. What kind of fluid loss is happening here?
explanation: Exactly! It's called 'insensible' because we can't easily measure it with a jug or a catheter—it just silently evaporates away through breath and skin.

question: Which of these is NOT a sign that a patient is lacking fluid (fluid volume deficit)?
explanation: You're doing great! Bounding pulses mean there is plenty of fluid pumping around (or too much!). Dehydration actually causes weak, thready pulses.

question: Why do patients with severe fluid overload often develop crackling sounds in their lungs?

options.A: Dehydration causes the bronchial tubes to narrow and whistle
options.B: Fluid backs up into the pulmonary air sacs and airways
options.C: The chest muscles weaken from holding extra body weight
options.D: The patient develops a secondary bacterial pneumonia infection

explanation: Spot on! When the plumbing system is overloaded, fluid backs up into the tiny air sacs (alveoli) in the lungs, making a crackling sound when they breathe.

question: What is considered the absolute best and most sensitive daily clue that a patient is gaining or losing fluid?
explanation: You got it! Scales don't lie. Weighing a patient at the same time every day gives us the fastest, most reliable warning sign of fluid changes.

question: A heart failure patient gains two kilograms in just 24 hours. Roughly how much excess fluid have they held onto?
explanation: Fantastic! Remember this handy nursing rule: one kilogram of body weight equals roughly one liter of fluid. A 2kg jump means about 2 extra liters of water!
